learn.hook: A car's speedometer shows 60 km/h at this very instant — but speed is distance over time, and an instant has no time. Calculus resolves this puzzle with limits.
points: Calculus studies how quantities change. Its two pillars are limits and derivatives; derivatives are built from limits.
Average velocity between t₁ and t₂ is [s(t₂) − s(t₁)]/(t₂ − t₁).
For a falling body, s = 4.9t² (metres, seconds). Between t = 2 and t = 2 + h, the average velocity is [4.9(2 + h)² − 4.9 × 4]/h = 19.6 + 4.9h.
As h gets closer and closer to 0, the average velocity gets closer to 19.6 m/s: the instantaneous velocity at t = 2.
In general the derivative is the limiting value of the average rate of change over shrinking intervals.

example.q: For s = 4.9t², find the average velocity from t = 2 s to t = 2.1 s, and guess the velocity at t = 2 s.
steps: Shorter intervals (h = 0.01: 19.649 m/s; h = 0.001: 19.6049 m/s) approach 19.6.
example.answer: 20.09 m/s; instantaneous velocity at t = 2 s is 19.6 m/s

learn.reallife: A cricket speed gun measures the ball's position at tiny time gaps and divides — a real-life version of shrinking the interval h towards 0.

games.title: From average to instantaneous velocity
items: Measure distance at t and at t + h
Average velocity = change in distance ÷ h
The averages approach one fixed value
That limiting value is the instantaneous velocity

games.title: Average velocity of s = 4.9t² from t = 2 to t = 2 + h, using 19.6 + 4.9h

quiz.q: For s = 4.9t², what is the average velocity between t = 0 and t = 2 (in m/s)?
quiz.mistake: Gives the instantaneous velocity at t = 2

quiz.q: For s = 4.9t², the instantaneous velocity at t = 2 s, in m/s, is:
quiz.mistake: Uses an average over a non-zero interval

quiz.q: Instantaneous velocity is obtained by:
options: dividing total distance by total time
putting h = 0 directly in [s(t + h) − s(t)]/h
taking the limit of average velocities as the time interval shrinks to 0
averaging the start and end velocities
quiz.explain: Putting h = 0 gives 0/0; we need the limit as h → 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks we can just substitute h = 0

quiz.q: A car travels s = t² metres in t seconds. What is its average velocity from t = 3 to t = 5 (in m/s)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the time interval

quiz.q: For s = t², the average velocity from t = 3 to t = 3 + h is 6 + h. The velocity at t = 3, in m/s, is:
Which two ideas form the foundation of calculus in this chapter?
quiz.explain: Derivatives are defined as limits of rates of change.

quiz.q: In [s(2 + h) − s(2)]/h, why can't we simply set h = 0?
options: Because the answer would be infinity
Because the expression becomes 0/0, which is undefined
Because s is not defined at 2
quiz.explain: At h = 0 both numerator and denominator are 0; only the limit is meaningful.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the answer would just be 0

quiz.q: A balloon's radius r (cm) after t seconds is r = 2t. Its average rate of growth between t = 1 and t = 4, in cm/s, is:
quiz.explain: (8 − 2)/(4 − 1) = 2 cm/s. For a linear function the average rate equals the instantaneous rate.
quiz.mistake: Divides the final radius by the final time only

teach.ask: Gappu asks: how can a speedometer show speed at one instant when speed is distance divided by time? Explain the idea of instantaneous velocity.
teach.praise: Shrink the time gap and see what the averages approach — that's the speed at an instant. Limits rule!
teach.nudge: What happens to the average velocity as you make the time interval smaller and smaller?

topics.title: Limits: left, right and from graphs

learn.hook: Walking towards a cliff edge from the left and from the right, do you arrive at the same height? If not, the limit there doesn't exist.
points: lim(x→a) f(x) = l means f(x) gets as close as we like to l when x is close enough to a (x ≠ a).
Left-hand limit (LHL): x → a⁻ (from values below a). Right-hand limit (RHL): x → a⁺ (from above).
The limit exists exactly when LHL and RHL both exist and are equal. The limit may differ from f(a), or exist even if f(a) is undefined.
Tables and graphs: read the values of f(x) as x approaches a from both sides.
For |x|/x: LHL at 0 is −1 and RHL is 1, so lim(x→0) |x|/x does not exist. For [x] at an integer n: LHL = n − 1, RHL = n.

example.q: Let f(x) = x + 2 for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = 3x − 1 for x > 1. Does lim(x→1) f(x) exist?
example.answer: No, the limit does not exist at x = 1

learn.reallife: Income-tax slabs make the tax RATE jump: the rate just below a slab boundary differs from the rate just above it, so the rate function has LHL ≠ RHL at each boundary.

games.title: Does the limit exist?
items: A limit can exist at a point where the function is not defined.
e.g. (x² − 1)/(x − 1) has limit 2 at x = 1 though f(1) is undefined.
If LHL = RHL = 5, the limit is 5.
That is the definition of the limit existing.
The limit ignores the value at a; they may differ.

quiz.q: f(x) = 3x + 2 for x ≤ 0 and 2(x + 1) for x > 0. What is lim(x→0) f(x)?
quiz.explain: LHL = 2 and RHL = 2(0 + 1) = 2; they are equal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks two formulas always mean no limit

quiz.q: What is lim(x→0⁻) |x|/x?
For f(x) = [x], what is the right-hand limit at x = 3?
For f(x) = [x], does lim(x→3) f(x) exist?
f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2), x ≠ 2. A table gives f(1.99) = 3.99 and f(2.01) = 4.01. The limit as x → 2 is:
quiz.explain: Both sides approach 4; indeed f(x) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the limit cannot exist because f(2) is undefined

quiz.q: f(x) = x² + 1 for x ≤ 1 and 3 − x² for x > 1. What is lim(x→1) f(x)?
quiz.explain: LHL = 1 + 1 = 2 and RHL = 3 − 1 = 2. They agree, so the limit is 2.
quiz.mistake: Uses only one of the two formulas

quiz.q: Which statement about lim(x→a) f(x) is correct?
options: It exists exactly when f(a) is defined
It exists exactly when LHL and RHL exist and are equal
quiz.explain: The value at a itself plays no part in deciding the limit.
quiz.mistake: Ties the limit to the function's value at a

quiz.q: f(x) = 5 for x ≠ 2 and f(2) = 7. What is lim(x→2) f(x)?
quiz.explain: Near 2 (but not at 2) the function is 5 on both sides.
quiz.mistake: Uses the value at the point itself

teach.ask: Gappu thinks the limit at x = a is always f(a). Explain left-hand and right-hand limits and when a limit exists.
teach.praise: Approach from both sides — if they agree, there's a limit, whatever f(a) is. Gappu gets it!
teach.nudge: What must be true about the left and right limits for the limit to exist?

topics.title: Algebra of limits; polynomials and rational functions

learn.hook: Most limits in board exams fall in 2 minutes: substitute, and if you get 0/0, factorise and cancel.
points: If lim f = l and lim g = m (as x → a): lim (f ± g) = l ± m, lim fg = lm, lim (f/g) = l/m (m ≠ 0), lim (λf) = λl.
Polynomials: lim(x→a) p(x) = p(a) — just substitute.
Rational function p/q: if q(a) ≠ 0, the limit is p(a)/q(a).
If substitution gives 0/0, factor (x − a) out of the top and bottom, cancel, then substitute.
Example: lim(x→3) (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = lim (x + 3) = 6.
learn.reallife: Economists find the marginal cost as a limit of (C(x + h) − C(x))/h; for polynomial cost models the algebra of limits makes this quick.

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→3) (5x − 1)/(x + 2).
Evaluate lim(x→5) (x² − 25)/(x − 5).
Evaluate lim(x→1) (x² + x − 2)/(x² − 1).
If lim(x→a) f(x) = 4 and lim(x→a) g(x) = −2, what is lim(x→a) [3f(x) − g(x)]?
Evaluate lim(x→0) [(x + 1)⁴ − 1]/x.
quiz.explain: Expand: (x + 1)⁴ − 1 = 4x + 6x² + 4x³ + x⁴; divide by x and let x → 0 to get 4.

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→π) (x² − 10).
quiz.explain: A polynomial: substitute x = π. Since π² ≈ 9.87, the answer is a small negative number, not 0.

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→3) (x³ − 27)/(x² − 9).
quiz.mistake: Cancels without factoring the cube correctly

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→2) (x² − 5x + 6)/(x − 2).

teach.ask: Gappu substituted x = 3 into (x² − 9)/(x − 3) and got 0/0, so he wrote 'no limit'. Explain the factor-and-cancel method.
teach.praise: 0/0 is a hint, not a dead end: factor, cancel, substitute. The answer is 6!
teach.nudge: What can you do when direct substitution gives 0/0?

topics.title: The xⁿ limit theorem, rationalising, and unknown constants

learn.hook: One theorem — lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ — kills a whole family of limits in a single line.
points: Theorem: for any positive integer n, lim(x→a) (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ (in fact it holds for any rational n with a > 0).
Ratio form: lim(x→1) (xᵐ − 1)/(xⁿ − 1) = m/n (divide top and bottom by x − 1).
Roots: multiply by the conjugate. lim(x→0) (√(1 + x) − 1)/x = lim 1/(√(1 + x) + 1) = 1/2.
Finding a constant: if the limit must exist, make LHL = RHL (for piecewise f) and solve.
Always check the final answer by substitution after simplifying.
learn.reallife: Pharmacologists model drug concentration with power functions; the xⁿ limit gives the instantaneous rate of change at any dose.

games.title: Evaluate lim(x→0) (√(1 + x) − 1)/x
items: Multiply top and bottom by √(1 + x) + 1

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→2) (x⁵ − 32)/(x − 2).
Evaluate lim(x→1) (x¹² − 1)/(x⁴ − 1).
Evaluate lim(x→0) (√(4 + x) − 2)/x.
If lim(x→2) (xⁿ − 2ⁿ)/(x − 2) = 80 and n is a positive integer, then n is:
f(x) = kx + 1 for x ≤ 2 and 3x − 1 for x > 2. For which k does lim(x→2) f(x) exist?
Evaluate lim(x→0) [√(1 + x) − √(1 − x)]/x.
quiz.explain: Multiply by the conjugate: 2x/(x[√(1 + x) + √(1 − x)]) → 2/2 = 1.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the factor 2 from (1 + x) − (1 − x)

quiz.q: f(x) = a + 2x for x < 1, 5 at x = 1, b − x for x > 1. If lim(x→1) f(x) = f(1), find a + b.
quiz.explain: LHL = a + 2 = 5 gives a = 3; RHL = b − 1 = 5 gives b = 6. So a + b = 9.
quiz.mistake: Finds only one of the constants

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→a) (x^(2/3) − a^(2/3))/(x − a), a > 0.
quiz.explain: The theorem n aⁿ⁻¹ holds for rational n with a > 0: (2/3)a^(−1/3).
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract 1 from the power

teach.ask: Gappu must evaluate lim(x→2) (x⁵ − 32)/(x − 2) and lim(x→0) (√(1 + x) − 1)/x. Explain the xⁿ theorem and the rationalisation trick.
must: n times a to the n minus 1
teach.praise: x⁵ − 32 over x − 2 → 5 × 2⁴ = 80, and the conjugate rescues the root limit. Smashing!
teach.nudge: In lim (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a), which formula gives the answer?

learn.hook: Type sin(0.001) into a calculator in radian mode: 0.00099999983… Almost exactly 0.001. That's the most famous limit in maths: sin x/x → 1.
points: Sandwich (squeeze) theorem: if g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) near a and lim g = lim h = l, then lim f = l.
lim(x→0) sin x/x = 1 (x in radians). Proof: in a unit circle, compare the areas of an inner triangle, a sector and an outer (tangent) triangle to get cos x < sin x/x < 1/cos x, then squeeze.
lim(x→0) (1 − cos x)/x = 0, since (1 − cos x)/x = 2 sin²(x/2)/x = sin(x/2) · [sin(x/2)/(x/2)] → 0 × 1.
Useful forms: sin ax/(bx) → a/b; tan x/x → 1; sin ax/sin bx → a/b.
(cos 2x − 1)/(cos x − 1) = sin²x/sin²(x/2) → 4 as x → 0.
learn.reallife: Pendulum clocks rely on sin θ ≈ θ for small angles — the reason small swings take almost the same time.

games.title: Prove lim(x→0) sin x/x = 1 (for 0 < x < π/2)
items: In a unit circle: area of inner triangle < area of sector < area of outer tangent triangle
½ sin x cos x < ½ x < ½ tan x
Divide by ½ sin x (positive): cos x < x/sin x < 1/cos x
Take reciprocals: cos x < sin x/x < 1/cos x
Both bounds tend to 1, so by the sandwich theorem sin x/x → 1

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) sin 5x/(3x).
Evaluate lim(x→0) tan 2x/x.
Evaluate lim(x→0) (cos 2x − 1)/(cos x − 1).
quiz.mistake: Cancels the cosines directly to get 2

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (1 − cos x)/x.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with lim sin x/x = 1

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (1 − cos 2x)/x².
quiz.explain: 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin²x, so the limit is 2[sin x/x]² → 2.

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) sin ax/sin bx (a, b ≠ 0).
The sandwich theorem is used to prove lim sin x/x = 1 because:
options: x is always larger than sin x
sin x/x is squeezed between cos x and 1/cos x, both of which tend to 1
quiz.explain: From cos x < sin x/x < 1/cos x and cos x → 1, the middle function must also tend to 1.

quiz.q: Evaluate lim(x→0) (x cos x + sin x)/x.

teach.ask: Gappu's calculator in radian mode shows sin(0.001)/0.001 ≈ 1. Explain why lim sin x/x = 1 and how to use it for sin 4x/sin 2x.
teach.praise: Squeezed between cos x and 1/cos x, sin x/x has nowhere to go but 1. And matching angles does the rest!
teach.nudge: To use lim sin x/x = 1 for sin 4x, what must the denominator look like?

learn.hook: The steepness of a mountain road at exactly one spot — that's the slope of the tangent, and it's the derivative.
points: Derivative of f at x = a: f′(a) = lim(h→0) [f(a + h) − f(a)]/h, if the limit exists.
The derivative function: f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h. Notations: f′(x), dy/dx, d/dx f(x), y′.
Using the definition directly is called finding the derivative from first principles.
Results: d/dx(x²) = 2x; d/dx(1/x) = −1/x²; d/dx(√x) = 1/(2√x); d/dx(sin x) = cos x; d/dx(cos x) = −sin x.
Geometric meaning: f′(a) is the slope of the tangent to y = f(x) at (a, f(a)).

example.q: Find the derivative of f(x) = 1/x from first principles.

learn.reallife: ISRO engineers use derivatives of position to get a rocket's instantaneous velocity and acceleration during launch.

games.title: Derivative of sin x from first principles

quiz.q: Using first principles, the derivative of f(x) = 3x² − 4x at x = 2 is:
What is the slope of the tangent to y = x² at x = 3?
Which limit defines f′(a)?
quiz.explain: It is the limit of the average rate of change as h → 0.

quiz.q: From first principles, d/dx(√x) is:
The derivative of a constant function f(x) = 7 is:
quiz.explain: f(x + h) − f(x) = 0 for all h, so the limit is 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the derivative of a constant is the constant

quiz.q: For f(x) = 1/x, what is f′(2)?
From first principles, d/dx(x³) is:
The derivative of f(x) = x at x = 5 is:

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know the steepness of y = x² at x = 3, exactly. Explain the first-principles definition of the derivative and what it means on a graph.
teach.praise: The derivative is the limiting slope as h shrinks — the slope of the tangent. At x = 3 it's 6!
teach.nudge: What happens to h in the definition, and what does the answer represent on the graph?

learn.hook: Nobody differentiates (x⁵ + 3x² − 7)(x² + 1) from first principles in an exam. A handful of rules does it in seconds.
points: Sum/difference: (u ± v)′ = u′ ± v′. Constant multiple: (cu)′ = cu′.
Product (Leibnitz) rule: (uv)′ = u′v + uv′.
Quotient rule: (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v², v ≠ 0.
Power rule: d/dx(xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹ for every positive integer n (proved using the binomial theorem). So d/dx(aₙxⁿ + … + a₁x + a₀) = naₙxⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₁.
Syllabus note: the chain rule is only assessed formatively in this chapter; expand composite expressions instead (e.g. (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1).

steps: u = x² + 1, u′ = 2x; v = x³ − 2x, v′ = 3x² − 2.

learn.reallife: An e-commerce startup's revenue R(p) = p × demand(p); the product rule gives the marginal revenue that pricing teams track.

quiz.q: d/dx(x⁷) is:
Differentiate f(x) = 4x³ − 3x² + 2x − 5 and find f′(1).
quiz.mistake: Keeps the constant −5 in the derivative

quiz.q: Using the product rule, d/dx[(x + 2)(x − 3)] is:
Using the quotient rule, d/dx[x/(x + 1)] is:
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order in the numerator

quiz.q: If y = (2x + 1)², find dy/dx at x = 1 by expanding first.
quiz.mistake: Gives 2(2x + 1) = 6, forgetting the factor 2 from inside

quiz.q: The derivative of f(x) = 1 + x + x²/2 + x³/3 at x = 1 is:
Which is the product (Leibnitz) rule?
quiz.explain: Each factor is differentiated in turn while the other is kept.

quiz.q: For f(x) = x¹⁰⁰ + x⁹⁹ + … + x + 1, what is f′(1)?
quiz.mistake: Counts the terms instead of adding the powers

teach.ask: Gappu must differentiate (x² + 1)(x³ − 2x) and x/(x + 1). Explain the product rule, the quotient rule and the power rule.
teach.praise: Power rule for each term, product rule for products, quotient rule for fractions. Differentiation dojo complete!
teach.nudge: In the quotient rule, what goes in the denominator?

topics.title: Derivatives of trigonometric functions and mixed problems

learn.hook: Sine becomes cosine, cosine becomes minus sine, tangent becomes sec². With the product and quotient rules, every trig derivative is within reach.
points: d/dx(sin x) = cos x; d/dx(cos x) = −sin x; d/dx(tan x) = sec²x (from tan x = sin x/cos x and the quotient rule).
d/dx(sec x) = sec x tan x; d/dx(cosec x) = −cosec x cot x; d/dx(cot x) = −cosec²x.
Products and quotients: e.g. d/dx[x⁴(5 sin x − 3 cos x)] = 4x³(5 sin x − 3 cos x) + x⁴(5 cos x + 3 sin x).
Linear fractions: d/dx[(ax + b)/(cx + d)] = (ad − bc)/(cx + d)².
Simplify with identities before or after differentiating, e.g. sin²x + cos²x = 1.

example.q: Find the derivative of tan x using the quotient rule.
steps: (cos x · cos x − sin x · (−sin x))/cos²x.

learn.reallife: Wave and vibration analysis in civil engineering (bridges, metro tracks) differentiates sine and cosine terms to find velocities and accelerations.

games.title: Differentiate sec x = 1/cos x
items: Quotient rule with u = 1, v = cos x

quiz.q: d/dx(x sin x) is:
d/dx[(ax + b)/(cx + d)] is:
quiz.explain: Quotient rule: [a(cx + d) − (ax + b)c]/(cx + d)² = (ad − bc)/(cx + d)².
quiz.mistake: Swaps the order in the numerator

quiz.q: d/dx(cot x) is:
quiz.explain: cot x = cos x/sin x: [(−sin x)(sin x) − cos x cos x]/sin²x = −1/sin²x.

quiz.q: If y = sin x + cos x, what is dy/dx at x = 0?
d/dx[x⁴(5 sin x − 3 cos x)] equals:
options: 4x³(5 sin x − 3 cos x) + x⁴(5 cos x − 3 sin x)
4x³(5 sin x − 3 cos x) + x⁴(5 cos x + 3 sin x)
quiz.explain: Product rule; d/dx(−3 cos x) = +3 sin x.
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of the derivative of cos x wrong

quiz.q: d/dx(sin x/x) is:
quiz.explain: Quotient rule: (cos x · x − sin x · 1)/x².

quiz.q: If f(x) = sec x, what is f′(0)?
quiz.explain: f′(x) = sec x tan x = 1 × 0 = 0 at x = 0.

quiz.q: Find d/dx[(x + 1)/(x − 1)] at x = 3.

teach.ask: Gappu keeps forgetting which trig derivatives have minus signs. Explain the six trig derivatives and how to get tan x from the quotient rule.
teach.praise: sin → cos, cos → −sin, tan → sec². The 'co' ones all get a minus. Memory locked!
teach.nudge: Which trig functions have derivatives with a minus sign in front?
